newsitem.title: POLAND: Revelations rock Polish security, ex-chief says.
newsitem.headline: Revelations rock Polish security, ex-chief says.

text.p: Poland's security service will take 15 years to recover from the leftist government's publication of a "White Book" of top-secret documents in the so-called Oleksy affair, its former chief said on Tuesday.

The government said the publication on Monday was meant to let the public judge how flimsy were the grounds on which Polish security agents accused then Prime Minister Jozef Oleksy last year of having knowingly collaborated with Moscow spies.
It will put the 464-page book, packed with details of how Poland's counter-spies operate, on sale in selected bookshops.
Former State Security Bureau (UOP) chief Gromoslaw Czempinski told Rzeczpospolita daily: "The White Book -- this is like a bitter joke -- is a wonderful present from the government to Russia.
"After this, the Polish services will have to be rebuilt over at least 15 years," added General Czempinski, who himself had to resign during the controversy over the issue.

Oleksy, while proclaiming his innocence, quit in January this year and now leads the ruling ex-communist party. Military prosecutors decided in April the evidence hastily gathered against him was so weak and flawed that they dropped the probe.
Polish media commentators and politicians, after studying the White Book, remained uncertain or divided over whether UOP agents had been justified in making their accusations.

The best-selling Gazeta Wyborcza daily said it was up to the UOP agents, and former Interior Minister Andrzej Milczanowski who announced the allegations to parliament in December, to confirm all relevant documents were in the book.

Justice Minister Leszek Kubicki said on Monday he had insisted that all the documents be included, cutting only some names or references which could endanger Polish secret operations or agents or harm witnesses and some bad language.
The allegations against Oleksy chiefly concerned his long acquaintance with Soviet and Russian diplomat Vladimir Alganov, who later proved to be a senior Moscow intelligence officer.
Oleksy has said these contacts were innocent if unwise.

He and his Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) party colleagues in government say the whole scandal was drummed up by UOP agents supporting Lech Walesa, who lost Poland's presidency to SLD leader Aleksander Kwasniewski in polls last year.
Some rightist opposition politicians accuse the government of a cover-up, while Czempinski has suggested Oleksy may have unwittingly let himself be used as a source by Moscow agents.
Walesa, who led the Solidarity union to its 1989 triumph over communism, said on Monday the White Book proved nothing.

He said the issue would only be resolved if the opposition won better representation in the now SLD-dominated parliament -- suggesting that the row over Oleksy will remain an issue in campaigning for general elections due in September 1997.
